framework.name: Illinois Learning Standards for English Language Arts (Common Core State Standards for ELA/Literacy)
framework.note: Codes name a strand, grade or grade band, and standard number (e.g. RL.3.1, W.9-10.7); the alignment was made by the course author and is not a certification by any agency.

standards.text: Hear and work with rhymes, syllables, and the separate sounds inside spoken words.
Tell long from short vowel sounds and blend, isolate, and segment the sounds in spoken one-syllable words.
Know how print works: left to right, top to bottom, letters make words, upper and lower case.
Match consonants to their primary sounds, link long and short vowel sounds to spellings, and read common sight words.
Use letter-sound knowledge, digraphs, and final-e patterns to decode one-syllable words.
Print many upper- and lowercase letters and use frequently occurring nouns and verbs when speaking and writing.
Decode regular words, common digraphs, inflectional endings, and irregularly spelled sight words.
Use vowel patterns, prefixes, suffixes, and sight-word knowledge to read grade-level words.
Read grade-level text accurately, at a good pace, and with expression, rereading as needed.
Use nouns, verbs, pronouns, and adjectives correctly and produce complete declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences.
Capitalize the first word of a sentence and the pronoun I, and recognize and name end punctuation.
Capitalize dates and names, use end punctuation, and spell common words correctly in writing.
Name the characters, settings, and major events in a story with prompting and support.
Ask and answer who, what, where, when, why, and how questions about a story's key details.
Retell stories, fables, and folktales and state the lesson or message they teach.
Compare two versions of the same story told by different authors or from different cultures.
Identify the main topic of an informational text and retell its key details.
Know and use text features such as headings, tables of contents, and glossaries to locate key facts.
Write a narrative that recounts two or more events in order using words like first and next.
Write an opinion about a topic or book, give a reason, and add a closing.
Write an informative piece that names a topic, gives facts about it, and closes.
Take part in conversations with peers and adults, follow turn-taking rules, and ask questions.
Tell a story or recount an experience with relevant facts and descriptive details, speaking audibly in coherent sentences.
Use words and phrases learned from conversations, reading, and being read to.
Decode words using common prefixes, suffixes, Latin suffixes, and multisyllable patterns.
Use sentence context, known affixes and roots, and glossaries to figure out unknown words.
Use context, Greek and Latin affixes and roots, and reference materials to find word meanings.
Determine the meaning of unfamiliar words through context, Greek and Latin roots, and reference tools.
Interpret similes, metaphors, and idioms and understand relationships among synonyms and antonyms.
Acquire and use grade-appropriate academic and domain-specific words, including words for precise actions, emotions, or states of being.
Recount fables, folktales, and myths from diverse cultures and explain the central message.
Describe a character's traits, motivations, and feelings and how actions affect the sequence of events.
Use details and examples from the text to explain what it says directly and to draw inferences.
Determine a theme from how characters respond to challenges and summarize the text.
Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view shapes the way events are described.
Explain differences among poems, drama, and prose using their structural elements when writing or speaking.
Determine the main idea of a text, explain how details support it, and summarize.
Use text features and search tools such as key words, sidebars, and hyperlinks to locate information efficiently.
Describe the overall structure of a text: chronology, comparison, cause and effect, or problem and solution.
Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
Interpret charts, graphs, diagrams, timelines, and other visual information and explain how they help.
Gather information from sources, take notes, categorize them, and provide a list of sources.
Write an opinion piece with a clear point of view, ordered reasons, linking words, and a conclusion.
Write an informative text that introduces a topic, groups related facts, and uses precise language.
Write a narrative with a situation, dialogue, description, transitions, sensory details, and a conclusion.
Develop and strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing, and rewriting with guidance.
Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis and reflection in writing.
Use capitals in titles, commas in addresses, and quotation marks in dialogue; apply spelling patterns.
Explain the function of nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs and produce simple, compound, and complex sentences.
Use relative pronouns, progressive tenses, and conventional adjective order; correct fragments and run-ons; use confused words like there and their.
Choose precise words and punctuation for effect and know when formal English is expected.
Come prepared to discussions, follow agreed rules, ask and answer questions, and build on others' remarks.
Paraphrase portions of information presented aloud or in other media formats.
Report on a topic or tell a story in an organized way with facts and details, speaking at an understandable pace.
Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports what a text says and the inferences drawn.
Analyze how particular elements of a story interact, such as how setting shapes characters or plot.
Explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker in a text.
Determine a theme and analyze its development through characters, setting, and plot; summarize objectively.
Compare a written story to its audio, film, or staged version and analyze the medium's effects.
Read and comprehend stories, dramas, and poems in the grades 6–8 complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed.
Determine two or more central ideas, trace their development, and write an objective summary.
Determine word meanings in a text and analyze how specific word choices affect meaning and tone.
Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations differently.
Trace and evaluate an argument, judging whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence relevant and sufficient.
Write arguments with clear claims, acknowledgment of opposing claims, logical reasoning, and relevant evidence.
Gather information from credible sources, quote or paraphrase without plagiarizing, and cite in a standard format.
Use context, Greek and Latin affixes and roots, and reference materials to determine word meanings.
Determine the meaning of unknown words using context, common roots and affixes, and reference tools.
Interpret figures of speech, understand word relationships, and distinguish connotations of similar words.
Interpret figures of speech such as verbal irony and puns and distinguish among words' connotations.
Determine figurative and connotative meanings in a text and analyze the effect of sound devices.
Acquire and use academic and domain-specific words and gather vocabulary knowledge when needed.
Use pronouns correctly in case, number, and person and recognize and correct inappropriate pronoun shifts.
Explain the function of phrases and clauses, use varied sentence types, and place modifiers correctly.
Explain the function of verbals, form and use active and passive voice, and use verb moods correctly.
Use commas, parentheses, or dashes to set off nonrestrictive elements and spell correctly.
Use a comma between coordinate adjectives and spell grade-appropriate words correctly.
Use a comma, ellipsis, or dash to indicate a pause or break and an ellipsis to show an omission.
Write arguments that introduce claims, address counterclaims, organize reasons logically, and use formal style.
Write informative texts that introduce and organize ideas with relevant facts, transitions, and precise language.
Write narratives using dialogue, pacing, description, and reflection, with a conclusion that follows from events.
Plan, revise, edit, rewrite, or try a new approach with guidance, focusing on purpose and audience.
Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
Cite strong and thorough textual evidence for explicit statements and inferences drawn from a text.
Determine a theme and analyze in detail how it emerges and is shaped by specific details.
Analyze how complex characters with conflicting motivations develop, interact, and advance the theme.
Analyze the cumulative effect of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including formal or informal tone.
Analyze how an author's structural choices, such as pacing and flashbacks, create effects like tension or surprise.
Analyze a subject or scene as represented in two different artistic mediums, noting what each emphasizes.
Analyze the cumulative impact of specific word choices on the meaning and tone of a text.
Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances that purpose.
Delineate and evaluate an argument's claims, reasoning, and evidence, identifying false statements and fallacies.
Analyze seminal U.S. documents of historical and literary significance and how they address related themes.
Write arguments with precise claims, fairly developed counterclaims, valid reasoning, and a formal style.
Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric, noting fallacious reasoning.
Determine word meanings using context, patterns of word changes, and reference materials including etymology.
Interpret figures of speech such as euphemism and oxymoron and analyze their role in a text.
Acquire and use academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for college and career readiness.
Determine figurative and connotative meanings of words and analyze their effect on meaning and tone.
Use parallel structure and various types of phrases and clauses to convey meaning and add variety.
Use a semicolon to link closely related independent clauses, a colon to introduce a list or quotation, and spell correctly.
Apply language knowledge in context and follow the guidelines in a style manual when writing.
Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, and rewriting for purpose and audience.
Produce clear, coherent writing whose development, organization, and style fit the task and audience.
Conduct short and sustained research projects to answer a question, synthesizing multiple sources.
Gather relevant sources, assess their usefulness, integrate information without plagiarizing, and cite them.
Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
Write informative texts that examine complex ideas through effective organization, evidence, and precise language.
Write narratives using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.
Strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing, and rewriting, focusing on what matters most for the purpose.
Cite strong textual evidence, including where the text leaves matters uncertain.
Determine two or more themes and analyze how they interact and build to produce a complex account.
Analyze the impact of an author's choices about setting, event order, and character development.
Analyze how choices about structure, such as where to begin or end, contribute to meaning and aesthetic impact.
Analyze a point of view requiring distinction between what is stated and what is meant, as in satire or irony.
Show knowledge of foundational American literature and how two or more texts from the same period treat similar themes.
Apply language knowledge to understand how it works in context and vary syntax for effect.
Analyze word choices with multiple meanings and language that is especially fresh, engaging, or beautiful.
Analyze how an author's style and content contribute to the power, persuasiveness, or beauty of a text.
Produce clear, coherent writing whose development, organization, and style fit task, purpose, and audience.
Strengthen writing by revising, editing, and rewriting, addressing what is most significant for the purpose.
Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text where the rhetoric is especially effective.
Integrate and evaluate multiple sources of information, including quantitative data, to address a question.
Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in seminal U.S. texts, including constitutional principles and public advocacy.
Analyze foundational U.S. documents such as the Declaration, Preamble, and Bill of Rights for themes and rhetoric.
Write arguments with precise, knowledgeable claims, counterclaims, valid reasoning, and sufficient evidence.
Evaluate a speaker's reasoning, evidence, stance, premises, and links among ideas, noting tone and word choice.
Understand that usage is a matter of convention that can change and resolve contested usage with references.
Observe hyphenation conventions and spell correctly when writing.
Vary syntax for effect and consult references for guidance when reading complex texts.
Produce writing whose development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
Plan, revise, edit, and rewrite, focusing on what is most significant for a specific purpose and audience.
Conduct sustained research projects, narrowing or broadening the inquiry and synthesizing multiple sources.
Gather authoritative sources, assess their strengths and limitations, avoid overreliance on one source, and cite properly.
Write arguments that support substantive claims with valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence.
Initiate and join collaborative discussions, probe reasoning and evidence, weigh diverse perspectives, synthesize claims, and resolve contradictions.
Present information and evidence so listeners can follow the reasoning, addressing alternative perspectives.
Make strategic use of digital media in presentations to enhance understanding and add interest.
